HISTORY & PHYSICAL (DETAILED)

Consult Summary:
32-year-old man with 4-day history of severe headache, subjective fever, generalized myalgias and a diffuse blanching pruritic rash after recent travel to Thailand; advised to attend an urgent in-person assessment to rule out travel-related arboviral infection (e.g., dengue) or other serious causes.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Severe, “very bad” headache for the past 4 days.  
• Timeline: Headache began first; subjective fever started later the same day. Symptoms persist without improvement.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Generalized aching muscles.  
  – Feels cold; no frank rigors.  
  – Diffuse red, itchy rash appearing “all over” body; blanching on glass test.  
• Pertinent negatives:  
  – No vomiting.  
  – No cough, coryza, or ear pain.  
  – No focal weakness; no pins & needles.  
  – No neck stiffness reported; photophobia question contradictory (patient initially said “yes” then immediately “no”—conflict noted).  
• Exposures: Returned from Thailand ≈1 week ago; multiple mosquito bites; travel companion also unwell.

Past Medical History:
• Denies any chronic medical conditions.  
• No prior surgeries mentioned.

Medications:
• Paracetamol – dose/route/frequency not documented (taken for headache).  
• Ibuprofen – dose/route/frequency not documented (taken for headache).  
Allergies:
• Denies drug or other allergies.

Social History:
• Recent foreign travel to Thailand.  
• Smoking, alcohol, occupation, recreational drug use – not discussed.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded (remote consultation).  
• General, HEENT, neuro, skin, cardio-resp, abdominal: Not recorded (no in-person exam).

Investigations:
• None to date; clinician recommended urgent face-to-face review with possible blood tests.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Acute febrile illness with severe headache, myalgias, and blanching diffuse rash following travel to a mosquito-endemic region; dengue fever highest on differential, but must exclude chikungunya, malaria, and early meningitis.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Dengue fever – supports: Thailand travel, mosquito bites, fever, severe headache, myalgias, blanching rash; opposes: no bleeding or retro-orbital pain yet.  
2. Chikungunya – supports: same travel exposure, rash and fever; opposes: lacks prominent arthralgias.  
3. Malaria – supports: endemic travel, fever/headache; opposes: blanching rash atypical, no cyclical pattern.

Issue 1: Suspected arboviral infection (dengue vs chikungunya)  
• Plan:  
  – Urgent in-person examination today at GP hub; if unavailable, present to Emergency Department.  
  – Labs to arrange after assessment: FBC (look for thrombocytopenia), LFTs, U&Es, dengue NS1/IgM serology, malaria rapid test & thick/thin films, blood cultures if febrile.  
  – Advise adequate oral hydration and continue antipyretics as needed.  
  – Provide strict return precautions for bleeding, worsening abdominal pain, dyspnea, or reduced urine output.

Issue 2: Rule-out meningitis / serious CNS infection  
• Plan:  
  – Neurologic and meningeal exam at face-to-face visit.  
  – If meningism, altered consciousness, or non-blanching rash develops, arrange immediate hospital transfer for lumbar puncture and IV antibiotics.  
  – Patient educated on “red flag” symptoms (photophobia, neck stiffness, confusion, non-blanching rash).

Issue 3: Symptom control  
• Continue paracetamol and ibuprofen as needed (avoid NSAIDs if dengue with thrombocytopenia confirmed – counsel to stop if bleeding or easy bruising).  
• Rest and monitor temperature.

General plan items:  
• Document vitals and physical findings at upcoming visit.  
• Consider infectious diseases referral depending on initial lab results.  
• Follow-up call within 24 h to ensure patient was reviewed.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: No vitals, physical exam, smoking/alcohol history, or family history obtained; will address at in-person visit.  
● Conflicts: Photophobia answer inconsistent within transcript; patient name recorded as “John” but clinician addressed “Ben.”  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio but brief; no objective data available.
